questions.stimulusTitle: Listening Part 1 · Announcement 1
questions.stimulusText: Attention all passengers on flight VN 245 to Da Nang. Due to ongoing runway maintenance, departure has been moved from Gate 12 to Gate 24. Boarding will commence at 14:15. Please have your boarding passes and identification ready.
questions.prompt: Where should passengers on flight VN 245 go for boarding?
questions.explanation: Đáp án C (Gate 24): Loa thông báo rõ 'departure has been moved from Gate 12 to Gate 24'. Bẫy nghe: Gate 12 là cổng cũ trước khi chuyển.

questions.stimulusTitle: Listening Part 1 · Announcement 2
questions.stimulusText: And now for the coastal regional forecast. A tropical depression moving northwest is bringing torrential rain and gale-force gusts up to 75 km/h. Small fishing vessels are strictly advised to seek immediate shelter and suspend operations until Thursday morning.

questions.explanation: Đáp án B (Small fishing boats): Bản tin nêu rõ 'Small fishing vessels are strictly advised to seek immediate shelter'.

questions.stimulusTitle: Listening Part 1 · Announcement 3

questions.explanation: Đáp án C (Save their work locally): Người thông báo nhắc nhở 'Please save all documents locally before 21:45'.

questions.stimulusTitle: Listening Part 2 · Conversation 1: University Course Enrollment & Part-time Work
questions.stimulusText:
Man: Hey Sarah, have you finalized your module choices for the upcoming semester yet?
Woman: Not quite, Mark. I'm torn between Advanced Macroeconomics and Corporate Financial Analysis. Both are rigorous, but Macroeconomics has lectures scheduled at 8 a.m. on Mondays and Thursdays.
Man: That sounds tough, especially since you work late shifts at the language center on Sunday evenings.
Woman: Exactly. If I take the early morning class, I’ll be completely exhausted. On the other hand, the Corporate Finance lecturer, Professor Harrison, is renowned for giving very practical project assignments that employers value.
Man: I had Professor Harrison last term. His workload is heavy—expect a 20-page group report and weekly case studies—but you learn far more real-world analytical skills.
Woman: That settles it then. I’d rather tackle demanding coursework at reasonable hours than struggle through 8 a.m. lectures after a night shift.
questions.prompt: What is Sarah's main concern regarding the Advanced Macroeconomics course?
options: The tuition fees are too high
The class meets very early in the morning
The professor has a poor reputation
It does not count toward her major
questions.explanation: Đáp án B: Sarah lo lắng vì 'Macroeconomics has lectures scheduled at 8 a.m. on Mondays and Thursdays' ngay sau ca làm tối chủ nhật.
questions.source: Đề thi chuẩn VSTEP Nghe Bậc 3-5 (QĐ 729/BGDĐT)

questions.stimulusTitle: Listening Part 2 · Conversation 2: Planning an Annual Corporate Seminar
questions.stimulusText:
Woman: Tom, our annual regional seminar is scheduled for mid-October, and we still haven't locked in the venue. We’re expecting around 150 attendees this year.
Man: Well, I shortlisted two candidates: the Grand Plaza Hotel in District 1 and the Riverside Convention Hub near the tech park.
Woman: What's the price comparison looking like?
Man: The Grand Plaza quoted $45 per delegate, which includes standard audiovisual equipment and morning refreshments. But their parking capacity is quite limited, and parking downtown is a nightmare.
Woman: Good point. What about Riverside?
Man: Riverside is slightly more expensive at $52 per head, but they offer complimentary shuttle service from the nearest metro station, spacious free parking, and state-of-the-art interactive digital podiums.
Woman: Since several keynote speakers are presenting complex live software demonstrations, reliable tech facilities and effortless guest arrival are paramount. Let's negotiate with Riverside to see if they can match $48 if we commit to their dinner banquet as well.
Man: Sound strategy. I’ll draft a revised proposal by this afternoon.
questions.prompt: How many attendees are projected for the seminar?
questions.explanation: Đáp án C: 'We’re expecting around 150 attendees this year'.
questions.source: Đề thi chuẩn VSTEP Nghe Bậc 3-5 (QĐ 729/BGDĐT)

questions.stimulusTitle: Listening Part 2 · Conversation 3: Apartment Lease & Maintenance Negotiation
questions.stimulusText:
Man: Good morning, Ms. Jenkins. I’m calling regarding the tenancy agreement for apartment 4B on Elm Street. I received the draft contract, but there are two clauses I’d like to clarify.
Woman: Certainly, Mr. Baker. What seems to be the issue?
Man: First, clause 7 states that the tenant is responsible for all plumbing and electrical repairs up to $200. Given that the water heater is over ten years old and already making rattling noises, I feel the landlord should cover pre-existing equipment maintenance.
Woman: That’s understandable. The landlord did mention replacing the heating unit before winter anyway. I can insert an addendum specifying that the boiler and core electrical circuits remain the owner's sole liability.
Man: That would be great. Second, regarding the security deposit: the agreement specifies two months' rent upfront, with return within 45 days after vacating. The standard municipal guideline is usually 30 days.
Woman: If the post-move-out inspection reveals no structural damage, our agency routinely processes deposit refunds within 21 business days. I can explicitly amend that to 30 calendar days in your agreement.
Man: Fantastic. Once you email the revised copy, I’ll sign and wire the deposit.
questions.prompt: Why is Mr. Baker concerned about clause 7?
options: The rent is scheduled to increase next month
The existing water heater is old and noisy
The landlord refused to provide furniture
He wants permission to keep a pet
questions.explanation: Đáp án B: 'the water heater is over ten years old and already making rattling noises'.
questions.source: Đề thi chuẩn VSTEP Nghe Bậc 3-5 (QĐ 729/BGDĐT)

questions.stimulusTitle: Listening Part 3 · Lecture 1: Urban Heat Islands & Sustainable Architecture
questions.stimulusText:
Good afternoon, students. Today we examine the Urban Heat Island effect—a phenomenon where metropolitan areas experience significantly higher ambient temperatures than surrounding rural landscapes. In dense cities, concrete, asphalt, and dark roofs absorb solar radiation during daylight and re-radiate this heat into the atmosphere long after sunset. Compounding this thermal mass is anthropogenic waste heat generated by millions of air conditioning compressors, combustion engines, and industrial factories.

Now, how are modern urban planners mitigating this thermal entrapment? Traditional approaches simply called for more air conditioning, which paradoxically exacerbates the problem by exhausting hot air onto city streets while consuming enormous electrical loads. Contemporary sustainable architecture takes a radically different route: passive thermal regulation.

First, consider the widespread adoption of 'green roofs' and vertical gardens. Vegetated surfaces mitigate heat through evapotranspiration—a natural biological process where plants absorb solar energy to evaporate water from leaves, thereby chilling the surrounding air microclimate. Second, materials science has engineered 'cool pavement' technologies. By embedding reflective polymers and light-colored micro-aggregates into asphalt, pavements can reflect up to 40% of solar radiation instead of absorbing it.

Finally, municipal zoning now prioritizes urban wind corridors. By arranging high-rise towers in staggered configurations parallel to prevailing seasonal breezes, cool marine or mountain air is funneled through central business districts, flushing out accumulated hot air pockets without mechanical power.
questions.prompt: What is a primary cause of the Urban Heat Island effect described in the lecture?
options: Solar heat absorption and re-radiation by concrete and asphalt
A complete absence of public transportation
questions.explanation: Đáp án B: 'concrete, asphalt, and dark roofs absorb solar radiation during daylight and re-radiate this heat into the atmosphere'.
questions.source: Đề thi chuẩn VSTEP Nghe Bậc 3-5 (QĐ 729/BGDĐT)

questions.stimulusTitle: Listening Part 3 · Lecture 1: Urban Heat Islands & Sustainable Architecture
questions.stimulusText:
Good afternoon, students. Today we examine the Urban Heat Island effect—a phenomenon where metropolitan areas experience significantly higher ambient temperatures than surrounding rural landscapes. In dense cities, concrete, asphalt, and dark roofs absorb solar radiation during daylight and re-radiate this heat into the atmosphere long after sunset. Compounding this thermal mass is anthropogenic waste heat generated by millions of air conditioning compressors, combustion engines, and industrial factories.

Now, how are modern urban planners mitigating this thermal entrapment? Traditional approaches simply called for more air conditioning, which paradoxically exacerbates the problem by exhausting hot air onto city streets while consuming enormous electrical loads. Contemporary sustainable architecture takes a radically different route: passive thermal regulation.

First, consider the widespread adoption of 'green roofs' and vertical gardens. Vegetated surfaces mitigate heat through evapotranspiration—a natural biological process where plants absorb solar energy to evaporate water from leaves, thereby chilling the surrounding air microclimate. Second, materials science has engineered 'cool pavement' technologies. By embedding reflective polymers and light-colored micro-aggregates into asphalt, pavements can reflect up to 40% of solar radiation instead of absorbing it.

Finally, municipal zoning now prioritizes urban wind corridors. By arranging high-rise towers in staggered configurations parallel to prevailing seasonal breezes, cool marine or mountain air is funneled through central business districts, flushing out accumulated hot air pockets without mechanical power.
questions.prompt: What characterizes 'cool pavement' technology?
options: It consists entirely of dark rubber from recycled tires
It embeds reflective polymers that bounce back solar radiation
It requires constant underground water irrigation
It can only be used on pedestrian sidewalks
questions.explanation: Đáp án B: 'By embedding reflective polymers and light-colored micro-aggregates into asphalt, pavements can reflect up to 40% of solar radiation'.
questions.source: Đề thi chuẩn VSTEP Nghe Bậc 3-5 (QĐ 729/BGDĐT)

questions.stimulusTitle: Listening Part 3 · Lecture 2: The Neurobiology of Habit Formation & Basal Ganglia
questions.stimulusText:
Welcome to Cognitive Neuroscience. Today's lecture explores how routine behaviors are encoded in the brain—specifically looking at the basal ganglia and the psychological 'habit loop'. When you first attempt a novel task, such as parallel parking an automobile, your prefrontal cortex—the seat of executive function, conscious decision-making, and intense concentration—is operating at maximum metabolic capacity. Every adjustment of the steering wheel requires deliberate mental effort.

However, the human brain is fundamentally an energy-conservation organ. Repeating a sequence of actions triggers a neurological process called 'chunking'. The brain automates individual micro-behaviors into a single cohesive motor script, and executive control shifts away from the prefrontal cortex toward an evolutionarily primitive subcortical structure known as the basal ganglia.

Researchers at MIT identified that all habits hinge upon a three-phase neurological loop: the Cue, the Routine, and the Reward. The 'Cue' is an environmental or emotional trigger that prompts the basal ganglia to select a subconscious script. The 'Routine' is the behavior itself, carried out almost involuntarily. Finally, the 'Reward' provides a surge of the neurotransmitter dopamine, cementing the neural pathway.

Crucially, modern neuroplasticity research confirms that an ingrained neural pathway is never truly deleted. When an individual attempts to extinguish an unhealthy habit through sheer willpower, the prefrontal cortex eventually fatigues, causing the basal ganglia to default back to the old groove. The only scientifically validated method to alter a habit is not extinction, but 'substitution'—maintaining the identical cue and reward while deliberately rewiring the middle routine.
questions.prompt: Which brain region is heavily engaged when performing an unfamiliar, complex task?
questions.explanation: Đáp án B: 'When you first attempt a novel task... your prefrontal cortex—the seat of executive function... is operating at maximum metabolic capacity'.
questions.source: Đề thi chuẩn VSTEP Nghe Bậc 3-5 (QĐ 729/BGDĐT)

questions.stimulusTitle: Listening Part 3 · Lecture 3: Ancient Mesopotamian Irrigation & Environmental Degradation
questions.stimulusText:
In environmental history, civilizations are often viewed through the lens of technological triumph; however, early societies were extraordinarily vulnerable to ecological overreach. Today, we turn to ancient Mesopotamia—the fertile alluvial plain situated between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, often heralded as the cradle of agriculture and urban civilization.

Around 3500 BCE, Sumerian city-states flourished by constructing monumental canal systems. These intricate engineering works diverted glacial meltwaters to cultivate wheat and barley in an otherwise arid desert. Yet, this remarkable irrigation triumph contained the seeds of its own destruction. The Tigris and Euphrates carry high mineral salt loads. Furthermore, southern Mesopotamia features exceptionally flat topography and an extremely hot climate with minimal drainage.

As farmers repeatedly flooded their fields, standing water evaporated under the scorching sun, drawing subterranean saline groundwater to the surface. Over decades of intensive irrigation, white mineral crusts accumulated in the topsoil—a catastrophic soil degradation process known as salinization.

Cuneiform clay tablets provide poignant historical evidence of this ecological crisis. Around 3000 BCE, Sumerian harvest records show equal proportions of wheat and barley. However, wheat possesses very low salt tolerance, whereas barley can tolerate moderately brackish soils. By 2500 BCE, wheat accounted for less than 15% of agricultural output. By 1800 BCE, wheat had vanished entirely from southern Mesopotamian records, and crop yields per hectare had plummeted by more than 60%.

Unable to sustain its dense urban populations, Sumerian civilization experienced chronic famines, political fragmentation, and ultimate geopolitical collapse, shifting power northward toward less degraded regions like Babylon.
questions.prompt: What allowed Sumerian city-states to cultivate crops in an arid environment?
options: Monumental canal systems diverting river waters
questions.explanation: Đáp án B: 'Sumerian city-states flourished by constructing monumental canal systems. These intricate engineering works diverted glacial meltwaters'.
questions.source: Đề thi chuẩn VSTEP Nghe Bậc 3-5 (QĐ 729/BGDĐT)
